comparator.name: Computing Science
comparator.academicYear: 2026–2027 adopted OER; prospective curriculum pages are indicative
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–27 OER supersedes the inconsistent prospective pages. It requires 60 EC in year one, 69 EC compulsory in years two and three, one 12-EC choice theme, a minimum 15-EC minor, 12 EC free academic electives and a 12-EC bachelor thesis. The current OER adds AI-Assisted Development, Human-Computer Interaction, Information Retrieval and Sustainability & IT to the required core; the prospective year-two page omits these and describes a different two-of-three choice. The three specialist tracks are mutually exclusive. This pathway takes the first OER-listed Cyber Security track solely under the neutral tie-break and leaves actual minor and free-choice space open.

alternatives.concept: A substantial UCR computing and mathematics curriculum combines programming, software development, algorithms, networks, databases, data science and AI with statistical research and analysis of societal impacts. UCR does not offer the specialist cyber-security, cryptography, web-security and independent Computing Science thesis sequence that Radboud requires.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The generic Computing Science target does not identify a track. The current adopted OER lists Cyber Security, Software Science and Data Science as three equally formal 12-EC options without designating a general track. Its first-listed track is selected as a neutral tie-break, not for UCR fit.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Programming and discrete mathematics begin in 2026; mathematical methods and database study precede advanced computing. Introductory algorithms and linear algebra precede advanced algorithms and numerical work. All recorded prerequisites precede the courses that require them, and every course is available in its assigned term.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The core programme already implements the available software, mathematical and data directions. A second genuinely different cybersecurity programme would require cryptography, operating-system security, web-security and penetration-testing courses absent from the UCR workbook; swapping in adjacent law or ethics courses would misrepresent this specialist direction.

notes.text: Both curricula contain programming, algorithms, data analysis and computing systems. Radboud also requires a formal Cyber Security track with cryptography, operating-system and web security, broader formal-computing theory, and an independent Computing Science thesis. UCR cannot present its networks, AI ethics or other courses as substitutes for those specialist requirements.
